acmCertExpiry30Days.^description: You have {$COUNT} ACM certificate(s) expiring within 30 days. Certificates must be renewed before expiry to avoid service disruptions. For imported certificates, manually re-import the renewed certificate. For ACM-issued certificates, verify that DNS validation records are in place or respond to email validation requests.

acmCertExpired.^description: [Critical] You have {$COUNT} expired ACM certificate(s). Expired certificates cannot secure connections and will cause service failures if still associated with resources. Replace immediately with a valid certificate.

acmRSAKeyLength.^description: You have {$COUNT} ACM certificate(s) using RSA-1024 key algorithm, which is cryptographically deprecated. RSA keys must be at least 2048 bits. ECDSA (EC_prime256v1, EC_secp384r1) is preferred for better security and performance.

acmCertRenewalFailed.^description: [Action Required] You have {$COUNT} ACM certificate(s) with failed renewal. ACM attempted auto-renewal but could not complete validation. Check DNS CNAME records, CAA records, or respond to email validation. Without intervention, the certificate will expire.

acmCertRevoked.^description: [Critical] You have {$COUNT} revoked ACM certificate(s). A revoked certificate may indicate a security incident (key compromise, CA compromise). Investigate the revocation reason, replace the certificate immediately, and rotate any potentially compromised credentials.

acmCertExpiry90Days.^description: You have {$COUNT} ACM certificate(s) expiring within 90 days. Plan renewal activities. For ACM-issued certificates with DNS validation, renewal should happen automatically at 60 days. For imported or email-validated certificates, manual action is required.

acmCertNotInUse.^description: You have {$COUNT} issued ACM certificate(s) not associated with any AWS resource. These may be orphaned certificates from decommissioned services. Review and delete if no longer needed. Private CA certificates incur cost even when unused.
acmCertNotInUse.shortDesc: Certificate not associated with any resource

acmCertPendingValidation.^description: You have {$COUNT} ACM certificate(s) stuck in pending validation, timed out, or failed state. These represent incomplete certificate requests that should be cleaned up. Delete the request and re-create if still needed, ensuring DNS/email validation is properly configured.

acmCertRenewalIneligible.^description: You have {$COUNT} ACM-issued certificate(s) not eligible for automatic renewal. This typically means the certificate uses email validation. Migrate to DNS validation to enable automatic renewal and eliminate manual intervention risk.

acmCertNoTags.^description: You have {$COUNT} ACM certificate(s) without any tags. Tags are essential for cost allocation, ownership identification, automation, and attribute-based access control (ABAC). Add tags for environment, owner, application, and cost center at minimum.

acmWildcardCert.^description: [Informational] You have {$COUNT} wildcard ACM certificate(s). Wildcard certificates increase blast radius if compromised, can mask unauthorized subdomains, and may not meet compliance requirements (e.g., PCI DSS). Consider using specific domain certificates where feasible.

acmCertTransparencyDisabled.^description: You have {$COUNT} ACM certificate(s) with Certificate Transparency (CT) logging disabled. CT enables detection of mis-issued certificates. Browsers may show warnings for certificates not logged to CT. Enable CT logging unless there is a specific business reason to keep domain names private.

acmImportedCertNoAutoRenewal.^description: You have {$COUNT} imported ACM certificate(s) approaching expiry that require manual renewal. ACM cannot auto-renew imported certificates. Plan to obtain a renewed certificate from your CA and re-import it before expiry. Consider replacing with ACM-issued certificates where possible.

pcaCaCertExpiringOrFailed.^description: You have {$COUNT} AWS Private CA certificate authorities that have FAILED or EXPIRED, or whose CA certificate expires soon (within 365 days for a root CA, 90 days for a subordinate CA). When a CA certificate expires, every certificate it issued stops validating and the CA can no longer issue certificates. Rotating a root CA takes a long time because the new root must reach every trust store. Plan the renewal or replacement before the CA certificate expires.
pcaCaCertExpiringOrFailed.shortDesc: Private CA failed, expired or expiring soon

pcaRevocationNotConfigured.^description: You have {$COUNT} active AWS Private CA certificate authorities with neither CRL nor OCSP enabled. Without a way to check revocation, relying parties keep trusting a compromised or retired certificate until it expires. Enable CRL distribution or OCSP. If certificates are short-lived, use short-lived certificate mode instead.
pcaRevocationNotConfigured.shortDesc: Private CA has no CRL or OCSP revocation

pcaRootCaInWorkloadAccount.^description: [Heuristic] An active AWS Private CA root CA is in an account and Region that also has ACM certificates in use by AWS resources, which suggests the root sits in a workload account. Keep root CAs in a dedicated, tightly restricted PKI account, and let only subordinate CAs (shared through AWS RAM if needed) issue workload certificates. This limits who can reach the trust anchor. If this account is already a dedicated PKI account, you can ignore this finding.
pcaRootCaInWorkloadAccount.shortDesc: Root CA appears to live in a workload account
ref: [Using AWS RAM to share a private CA cross-account]<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/privateca/latest/userguide/pca-ram.html>
